notes.front: What problem does consensus solve, and what makes it fundamentally hard?
notes.back:
Getting N processes to agree on one value (or one ordered log) despite crashes and message delays.

Hard because in an asynchronous network a slow node is indistinguishable from a dead node. Any protocol must therefore risk either blocking forever (waiting) or deciding twice (acting on a false suspicion).

notes.front: State the Fischer–Lynch–Paterson (FLP) impossibility result. How do Raft and Paxos coexist with it?
notes.back:
No deterministic protocol can guarantee both safety (never two different decisions) and liveness (eventually decides) in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash failure.

Raft/Paxos guarantee safety unconditionally and liveness only under partial synchrony (timeouts eventually hold). Elections can in theory livelock forever; randomized timeouts make that improbable, not impossible.

notes.front: Why does tolerating f crash failures require 2f+1 nodes? Why 3f+1 for Byzantine?
notes.back:
Any two majorities of 2f+1 overlap in ≥1 node. That intersection is what carries decisions across leader changes. With f down you still have f+1 = majority, so progress continues.

Byzantine: the overlapping node might lie, so you need overlap of f+1 to guarantee at least one honest node in the intersection → 3f+1.

notes.front: Why is a quorum of “any 2 of 5” unsafe for consensus?
notes.back:
Two disjoint 2-of-5 sets can exist, so two leaders could each commit a different value at the same log index.

Safety requires every write quorum to intersect every other write quorum (and every read quorum, if reads bypass the leader). The formula for replicated reads/writes is R + W > N.

notes.front: Flexible Paxos: which quorums actually need to intersect, and what does that buy you?
notes.back:
Only the Phase 1 (prepare/leader-election) quorum and the Phase 2 (accept/replication) quorum must intersect: |Q1| + |Q2| > N. Phase 2 quorums need not intersect each other.

You can make Q2 small (fast, low-latency commits in steady state) at the cost of a larger Q1 (rare, on leader change). Same idea underlies Amazon Aurora's 4/6 write, 3/6 read quorums.

notes.front: Two Generals: why is exactly-once message delivery impossible over a lossy network?
notes.back:
Any acknowledgement can itself be lost, so neither side can ever be certain the other knows the message arrived. Induction: the last message is always dispensable, so no finite protocol reaches common knowledge.

Consequence: real systems offer at-least-once delivery + idempotent/deduplicated processing and call that “exactly-once” (Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) FIFO, Kafka transactions).

notes.front: Raft decomposes consensus into three sub-problems. Name them and the safety property that ties them together.
notes.back:
• Leader election
  • Log replication
  • Safety
State Machine Safety: if any server has applied entry i, no other server will ever apply a different entry at index i.

notes.front: What is a Raft term, and what problem does it solve without synchronized clocks?
notes.back:
A monotonically increasing logical clock. Each term has at most one leader. Every message carries the sender's term; a node that sees a higher term immediately updates and steps down to follower; messages with a stale term are rejected.

Terms let nodes detect obsolete leaders and stale information purely from message content — no wall-clock needed.

notes.front: Walk through a Raft leader election. Why are election timeouts randomized?
notes.back:
Follower hears nothing for an election timeout → becomes candidate, increments term, votes for itself, sends RequestVote to all. Wins on a majority, becomes leader, sends heartbeats. Loses if it sees a valid leader's AppendEntries with ≥ its term.

Randomized timeouts (paper: 150–300 ms) make simultaneous candidates rare, so split votes resolve quickly. This is Raft's practical answer to FLP livelock.

notes.front: Raft's election restriction: a voter denies a candidate whose log is less up-to-date. Define “up-to-date” and explain why this matters.
notes.back:
Compare last entry: higher term wins; same term → longer log wins.

It yields Leader Completeness: any committed entry is guaranteed to be in every future leader's log. The new leader never has to fetch missing committed entries — unlike Paxos, where a new leader must first learn previously chosen values. Data only flows leader → follower.

notes.front: State Raft's Log Matching Property and the mechanism that enforces it.
notes.back:
If two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, then (1) the entries are identical and (2) all preceding entries are identical.

Enforced by the AppendEntries consistency check: each RPC carries prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm; the follower rejects if its log doesn't match there, and the leader backs up nextIndex until they agree, then overwrites the follower's divergent suffix.

notes.front: Why can a Raft leader not commit an entry from a previous term merely by observing it on a majority? (Raft paper Figure 8)
notes.back:
An old-term entry replicated on a majority can still be overwritten: a later candidate whose last entry has a higher term can win election without holding that entry, then overwrite it. Counting replicas is only safe for current-term entries.

Rule: leaders commit only current-term entries by counting; prior entries commit transitively. Practical trick: a new leader appends a no-op entry immediately so earlier entries become committable.

notes.front: Why can't Raft switch cluster membership directly from C<sub>old</sub> to C<sub>new</sub>? What are the two safe approaches?
notes.back:
During the switch different servers would apply the change at different times, so a majority of Cold and a majority of Cnew could form two disjoint quorums in the same term.

  • Joint consensus: transitional config Cold,new where decisions require majorities of both.
  • Single-server changes: add/remove one server at a time — any two consecutive configs' majorities always overlap. etcd uses this (with learners for catch-up).

notes.front: What is a Raft learner (non-voting member) and why does etcd add new members as learners first?
notes.back:
A member that receives the log but doesn't count toward quorum.

Adding a fresh voter immediately raises the quorum size while the new node can't yet vote meaningfully (empty log) — a 3→4 node change temporarily makes the cluster less available. Learners catch up first, then get promoted.

notes.front: How does Raft serve a linearizable read? Name the two techniques and their trade-off.
notes.back:
• ReadIndex: leader records its commit index, exchanges one heartbeat round with a majority to prove it's still leader, then serves the read once the state machine reaches that index. Costs one network round trip; needs no clocks.
  • Lease-based reads: leader assumes it's still leader for one election timeout after its last successful heartbeat round. Zero extra round trips, but correctness depends on bounded clock drift.
Without either, a deposed leader in a partition could serve stale data. etcd defaults to ReadIndex; “serializable” reads skip it.

notes.front: PreVote and CheckQuorum in Raft (both used by etcd): what failure do they fix?
notes.back:
A follower cut off by a partial partition keeps timing out, incrementing its term and starting elections. When connectivity returns its inflated term forces the healthy leader to step down — a “disruptive server”.

  • PreVote: candidate first asks “would you vote for me?” without incrementing its term; only proceeds if a majority say yes.
  • CheckQuorum: a leader that can't reach a majority within an election timeout steps down itself, so a partitioned leader stops serving lease reads.

notes.front: Raft log compaction: how does snapshotting work and what RPC handles a lagging follower?
notes.back:
Each server independently snapshots its state machine up to a committed index and discards the log prefix. The snapshot stores the last included index/term (needed for AppendEntries checks) and the current membership.

If a follower is so far behind that the leader has discarded the entries it needs, the leader sends InstallSnapshot. In etcd, snapshots are also how new members bootstrap.

notes.front: Paxos roles: proposer, acceptor, learner. What does each do, and which role holds the safety-critical state?
notes.back:
• Proposer: drives a ballot, proposes a value.
  • Acceptor: votes; stores promisedBallot, acceptedBallot, acceptedValue on stable storage — this is the safety-critical state.
  • Learner: discovers which value was chosen (accepted by a majority).
In practice one process plays all roles.

notes.front: Describe the two phases of single-decree Paxos.
notes.back:
Phase 1 (Prepare/Promise): proposer picks a unique ballot n, sends Prepare(n). Acceptor promises to ignore anything < n and replies with the highest-ballot value it has already accepted (if any).

Phase 2 (Accept/Accepted): on a majority of promises, proposer sends Accept(n, v) where v = the highest-ballot accepted value returned, or its own value if none. Acceptors accept unless they've promised a higher ballot. Majority accepted ⇒ chosen.

notes.front: Why must a Paxos proposer adopt the highest-ballot value returned in Phase 1 instead of its own?
notes.back:
Once a value v is chosen (accepted by a majority M), any later Phase 1 majority M' intersects M, so at least one acceptor reports v (or a later ballot that, by induction, also carries v). Adopting the highest returned value guarantees every subsequent ballot re-proposes v.

This is the whole safety argument: chosen values are sticky. Skip it and two ballots can choose different values.

notes.front: Multi-Paxos: how does it amortize the protocol, and how does the resulting system differ from Raft?
notes.back:
Run Phase 1 once to establish a stable leader over a range of log slots; then each slot needs only Phase 2 (one round trip) — same steady-state cost as Raft.

Differences: Paxos permits holes and out-of-order acceptance in the log; a new leader must run Phase 1 per uncertain slot to learn chosen values. Raft forces a contiguous log and pushes all that work onto the election restriction. Paxos is more flexible; Raft is easier to get right.

notes.front: What is the Paxos dueling proposers problem, and how is it mitigated?
notes.back:
Two proposers keep issuing higher ballots; each Prepare invalidates the other's pending Accept → livelock (FLP in practice).

Mitigation: elect a distinguished proposer (leader) and/or randomized exponential backoff. Leader election is itself best-effort — a wrong guess costs liveness, never safety.

notes.front: Where does Amazon Web Services (AWS) run Paxos in production, and what pattern do these uses share?
notes.back:
• Amazon DynamoDB: each partition's replication group elects its leader with a Paxos-based protocol.
  • Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) control plane and internal lock/metadata services.
  • Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (ARC): routing-control state replicated with Paxos across five regions.
Pattern: Paxos guards a small, critical metadata/leadership plane; bulk data replication uses cheaper chain or quorum replication under that leader.

notes.front: Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (ARC) uses a Paxos cluster across five regions. What design principle does that illustrate?
notes.back:
The failover mechanism must be more available than the thing it fails over. The routing-control data plane is replicated across 5 regions and needs only a majority (3) to stay writable, so a regional outage cannot also disable your ability to fail out of that region.

Corollary: never put your failover switch on the same failure domain as the workload (e.g., in the primary region's control plane).

notes.front: Azure Storage architecture: where do Paxos and strong consistency come from?
notes.back:
Three layers per storage stamp: Front-End → Partition Layer (object semantics, range partitions) → Stream Layer (append-only extents).

Extents are replicated synchronously in a chain (write acked only when all 3 replicas persist); the Stream Manager tracks extent metadata using Paxos. All writes go through one partition server per range → Azure Storage is strongly consistent within a region and exposes ETags for optimistic concurrency.

notes.front: What consensus protocol does etcd use, and what is the Kubernetes (K8s) control plane's relationship to it?
notes.back:
Raft. etcd is the only stateful control-plane component; every Kubernetes object is a key under /registry/.... kube-apiserver is a stateless front-end that validates, serializes and does optimistic concurrency against etcd revisions.

So Kubernetes' control plane inherits Raft's properties: CP, majority-quorum availability, write latency ≥ one fsync + one majority round trip.

notes.front: Why do etcd clusters run 3 or 5 members, never 4 or 6?
notes.back:
Fault tolerance = ⌊(N−1)/2⌋. 4 members tolerate 1 failure — same as 3 — but add write latency (larger quorum) and one more machine whose failure counts. 5 tolerates 2. 7 is rarely worth the throughput cost of a 4-node quorum.

Managed control planes (Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS), Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)) spread the members across 3 Availability Zones.

notes.front: Why is etcd write latency bounded below by disk fsync, and what operational rule follows?
notes.back:
Every Raft log entry must be fsynced to the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) on a majority before the leader acks — otherwise a crash could lose a “committed” entry, violating safety.

Rule: dedicated low-latency SSD for etcd; watch wal_fsync_duration_seconds (p99 should stay under ~10 ms). Slow disks manifest as leader elections and apiserver timeouts, not as “disk errors”.

notes.front: etcd exposes linearizable vs serializable reads. Define both and say what kube-apiserver uses.
notes.back:
• Linearizable (default): goes through ReadIndex; reflects all writes committed before the read started, even during a leader change.
  • Serializable: served from the local member's state; can be arbitrarily stale on a partitioned member.
kube-apiserver issues quorum (linearizable) reads to etcd by default. Recent versions can serve consistent reads from the watch cache by using etcd progress notifications to confirm the cache has reached the current revision — a ReadIndex at the cache layer.

notes.front: How does the Kubernetes API implement optimistic concurrency, and what does that force every controller to do?
notes.back:
Each object carries metadata.resourceVersion (the etcd modification revision). An update must carry the version it read; apiserver performs a compare-and-swap against etcd and returns 409 Conflict if the object changed.

Consequence: controllers must re-read and retry (client-go RetryOnConflict). There are no cross-object transactions — every multi-step operation must be idempotent and reconciled, never assumed atomic.

notes.front: How do kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler replicas pick a leader, and why is this not consensus?
notes.back:
A Lease object (coordination.k8s.io) updated via compare-and-swap. Defaults: leaseDuration 15 s, renewDeadline 10 s, retryPeriod 2 s.

It relies on etcd for atomicity, but leadership is time-based: a leader that stalls (garbage-collection pause, VM freeze) may still believe it leads after the lease expired while a new leader acts. “At most one active leader” holds only if the leader stops itself before renewDeadline — and only for actions that are idempotent or protected by resourceVersion.

notes.front: What is a fencing token, and why are leases alone insufficient for mutual exclusion?
notes.back:
A monotonically increasing number issued with each lock/lease grant; every protected resource rejects requests carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen.

Scenario: A acquires lease, pauses (GC/VM stall), lease expires, B acquires, then A wakes and writes. Without fencing the storage happily accepts A's stale write. Kubernetes gives you resourceVersion/generation as usable tokens for API objects; external systems need their own.

notes.front: How does Kubernetes detect a dead node, and why does it deliberately act slowly?
notes.back:
kubelet renews a node Lease (~every 10 s). If the controller-manager sees no renewal within node-monitor-grace-period (~40–50 s), it marks the node NotReady; pods are evicted after tolerationSeconds (default 300 s).

Detection is timeout-based, so false positives are unavoidable: a partitioned kubelet is indistinguishable from a dead one. Slow reaction trades availability for not double-running workloads.

notes.front: Why will a StatefulSet not recreate a pod from an unreachable node until the old pod is confirmed deleted?
notes.back:
StatefulSets promise at-most-one pod per ordinal identity. The API cannot know whether pod-0 on the partitioned node is still running and writing to its volume. Creating a second pod-0 = split brain on the same persistent identity.

Force-deleting (--grace-period=0 --force) is the human asserting a fence (“I have verified the node is dead / powered off”). Cloud providers automate this fence by deleting the Node object when the instance is terminated.

notes.front: Kubernetes controllers are level-triggered, not edge-triggered. Why is that the right choice for a distributed system?
notes.back:
Edge-triggered = act on each event; a missed event (watch disconnect, restart, compaction → 410 Gone) leaves the system permanently wrong.
Level-triggered = observe current state, compute diff to desired state, act; converges from any starting point.

Watches are a latency optimization; periodic resync/relist is the correctness mechanism. This is how controllers tolerate lost messages without exactly-once delivery.

notes.front: What happens when an etcd member returns 410 Gone for a watch, and what does it teach about log compaction?
notes.back:
etcd compacts old revisions (apiserver default: every 5 min). A client resuming a watch from a compacted revision can't get the intermediate events and must relist from the current state.

Lesson: any replicated log is eventually truncated; consumers must be able to rebuild from a snapshot. Same reason Raft needs InstallSnapshot.

notes.front: etcd hits its space quota (default 2 GB; recommended max 8 GB). What happens to the Kubernetes cluster?
notes.back:
etcd raises a NOSPACE alarm and becomes read-only cluster-wide. Every Kubernetes write fails; running pods keep running, but nothing can be scheduled, scaled or updated.

Root causes: unbounded object growth (Events, Jobs, custom resources), missing compaction, no defrag after deletes. Fix: compact → defrag → disarm alarm. Illustrates a capacity failure that looks like a consensus failure.

notes.front: etcd across Availability Zones: compare a 2-AZ and 3-AZ layout for a 3-member cluster.
notes.back:
3 AZs, 1 member each: any single AZ loss leaves 2/3 → quorum intact.
2 AZs (2+1): losing the AZ with 2 members drops to 1/3 → no quorum, control plane down. Losing the other AZ is fine. Availability is asymmetric and the cluster is only as good as its worst AZ.

General rule: place members so that no single failure domain holds a majority.

notes.front: How should a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) be set for a quorum-based workload (etcd, ZooKeeper, Kafka KRaft) and why?
notes.back:
minAvailable = quorum size (e.g., 2 of 3, 3 of 5) or maxUnavailable: 1. Voluntary disruptions (node drain, cluster upgrade) then never take the replica set below majority.

PDBs only govern voluntary evictions. Combine with topology-spread constraints so an AZ outage (involuntary) can't remove a majority either.

notes.front: Kubernetes API objects have no multi-object transactions. How do you implement “create A, then B, and roll back if B fails”?
notes.back:
You don't roll back — you reconcile. Write desired state; a controller drives actual state toward it idempotently and repeatedly. Use ownerReferences for garbage collection, finalizers for ordered teardown, and status.conditions to publish progress.

This is coordination avoidance: instead of paying for a distributed transaction, design each step so repeating it is harmless.

notes.front: Amazon DynamoDB: describe the replication of a single partition and the two read consistency options.
notes.back:
Each partition has 3 replicas across 3 Availability Zones; a Paxos-elected leader accepts writes and acks after persisting on itself plus one more (2 of 3).

  • Eventually consistent read (default, half the Read Capacity Units (RCU)): any replica; may miss a just-committed write (typically <1 s).
  • Strongly consistent read: served by the leader; reflects every successful write before it. Not available on Global Secondary Indexes (GSI).

notes.front: Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables: what is the consistency model and how are conflicts resolved?
notes.back:
Multi-active, asynchronous cross-region replication (typically ~1 s). Conflicts resolved by last-writer-wins on a timestamp attribute — concurrent writes in two regions silently drop one.

Classic PA/EL. Strongly consistent reads are only region-local. Newer multi-Region strong consistency tables route writes through a cross-region quorum, buying linearizability at the cost of cross-region write latency — PACELC as a per-table setting.

notes.front: Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) became strongly consistent for read-after-write in Dec 2020. What did the old model allow, and why is the change notable?
notes.back:
Old: PUT of a new object was read-after-write consistent, but overwrites/deletes and LIST were eventual — you could read a stale version or see a deleted key listed.

New: every GET/LIST after a completed PUT/DELETE returns the latest state. Notable because they did it at S3 scale with no latency or price change, by making the metadata index/cache layer coherently versioned so caches can detect and bypass stale entries rather than serving them.

notes.front: Amazon Aurora storage: what are its write and read quorums and why exactly 6 copies?
notes.back:
6 copies across 3 Availability Zones (2 per AZ). Write quorum 4/6, read quorum 3/6 (4+3 > 6).

Design target “AZ+1”: survive an entire AZ loss plus one more failure without losing read availability (3 copies left ≥ read quorum), and survive an AZ loss without losing write availability (4 left = write quorum). Repairs use read quorum to rebuild the missing copies.

notes.front: Amazon Aurora Global Database vs Aurora Multi-AZ: place each on the CAP/PACELC map.
notes.back:
• Within a region: synchronous 4/6 quorum → CP, linearizable primary.
  • Global Database: storage-level asynchronous replication to secondary regions (typical lag <1 s). Secondaries serve stale reads (EL). Failover promotes a secondary and accepts data loss up to the replication lag — the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the staleness.
Lesson: the same product is CP locally and AP/EL globally; ask “consistent with respect to what boundary?”.

notes.front: Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) Multi-AZ failover flips a DNS name to the standby. What client-side failure mode does this create?
notes.back:
Clients that cached the old DNS answer (Java Virtual Machine (JVM) default is effectively forever, connection pools hold sockets) keep talking to the old primary — or hang.

Mitigations: honour DNS TTL, bound connection lifetime, or put Amazon RDS Proxy in front so failover is handled server-side. General rule: a failover that requires clients to notice is only half a failover.

notes.front: Define AWS's principle of static stability and give two examples.
notes.back:
A system keeps operating correctly when a dependency (usually a control plane) is unavailable, by not needing to call that dependency during the failure — it relies on state it already has.

  • EC2 instances keep running when the EC2 control plane is impaired; Amazon Route 53 keeps answering when its API is down.
  • Pre-provision capacity in every AZ so an AZ failure doesn't require launching instances (a control-plane call) to recover.
Kubernetes analogue: pods and Service routing keep working when etcd/apiserver are down.

notes.front: Explain shuffle sharding (Amazon Route 53, many AWS services). What blast radius does it achieve?
notes.back:
Assign each customer a random subset of k nodes out of N instead of a fixed shard. Two customers sharing all k nodes is combinatorially rare (for 8 nodes, k=2: only 1/28 pairs fully overlap; with retries a client needs just one healthy node).

A poison-pill request from one customer then degrades a tiny fraction of others rather than a whole shard. It is isolation achieved by statistics rather than by coordination.

notes.front: What is a cell-based architecture and why does it sidestep CAP-style trade-offs?
notes.back:
Partition a service into many independent, identically-shaped cells (each a full stack with fixed max size); a thin routing layer maps customers to cells. Cells share no state.

No shared state ⇒ no cross-cell coordination ⇒ no consensus or quorum across cells; a cell failure is bounded to its customers. Scale is added by adding cells, not by growing a quorum. Trade-off: cell migration and the routing layer become the hard problems.

notes.front: Retry storms: why do naive retries turn a slow dependency into an outage, and what is the AWS-recommended pattern?
notes.back:
A dependency at capacity gets slow → callers time out and retry → load multiplies (3 retries = 4× load) at exactly the moment capacity is lowest → collapse. With N layers each retrying, amplification is exponential.

  • Exponential backoff with full jitter (spreads retries; avoids synchronized waves).
  • Retry budgets: e.g., retries ≤10% of successful calls.
  • Retry only at one layer; circuit breakers; load shedding.

notes.front: Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) Standard vs FIFO: delivery and ordering guarantees, and what “exactly-once processing” really means.
notes.back:
• Standard: at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering, near-unlimited throughput.
  • FIFO: per-MessageGroupId ordering; “exactly-once processing” = at-least-once + content/ID-based deduplication within a 5-minute window.
Delivery is never exactly-once (Two Generals). Consumers must still be idempotent for anything beyond the dedup window or across crashes mid-processing.

notes.front: Amazon DynamoDB TransactWriteItems: how does it achieve atomicity across partitions and what does it cost?
notes.back:
A transaction coordinator runs two-phase commit (2PC) across the affected partitions' leaders: prepare (check conditions, reserve) then commit. The result is serializable across the items.

Cost: 2× write capacity units per item (both phases are persisted), higher latency, and items in a pending transaction reject conflicting transactions (TransactionConflict). Use only where atomicity across items is truly required.

notes.front: Amazon DynamoDB hot partition: what limits exist and how do you design around them?
notes.back:
Per-partition ceiling ≈ 3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU. A single hot key (celebrity user, current-day timestamp) saturates one partition even if the table has spare capacity elsewhere. Adaptive capacity helps but can't split a single key.

Fixes: write sharding (append a random/hash suffix to the key and scatter-gather on read), pre-aggregate, or cache with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX). A load-distribution problem, not a consistency problem.

notes.front: How do EC2 ClientToken / idempotency tokens turn at-least-once RPC into effectively-once?
notes.back:
Client generates a unique token per logical operation and sends it on every retry; the service stores token → result and returns the cached result for duplicates.

This moves deduplication to the receiver where the state lives — the only place it can be done correctly. Same mechanism as SQS FIFO dedup IDs and Stripe idempotency keys.

notes.front: List Azure Cosmos DB's five consistency levels from strongest to weakest.
notes.back:
• Strong — linearizable
  • Bounded staleness — lag ≤ K versions or ≤ T time
  • Session — read-your-writes, monotonic reads/writes, writes-follow-reads within a session token (the default)
  • Consistent prefix — never see writes out of order, may be stale
  • Eventual — no ordering guarantee, converges
Each step down buys lower latency and higher availability in multi-region deployments.

notes.front: Azure Cosmos DB bounded staleness: define it precisely and say when it degenerates to strong.
notes.back:
Reads may lag writes by at most K versions or T time interval, whichever is reached first; outside the window they honour consistent prefix and monotonic reads. Configured per account (e.g., K=100,000 ops or T=5 min for multi-region).

In a single-region account the window can't accumulate lag, so it behaves like strong consistency. Its value is giving quantified, predictable staleness across regions instead of a binary strong/eventual choice.

notes.front: Azure Cosmos DB session consistency: how is it implemented, and what mistake breaks it?
notes.back:
The client Software Development Kit (SDK) carries a session token (per-partition logical sequence numbers) on each request; the replica serving a read must have caught up to that token or forwards.

Breaks when the token isn't propagated: two microservice instances, a serverless function per request, or a web tier that doesn't pass the token back to the browser. Read-your-writes then silently becomes eventual. Guarantees are scoped to the token, not to the user.

notes.front: Azure Cosmos DB strong consistency across multiple regions: what does a write cost and what feature is incompatible?
notes.back:
Writes are committed to a majority quorum in the write region and then synchronously to a majority of regions; documented write latency ≈ 2 × RTT to the farthest region.

Incompatible with multi-region writes (multi-master): you can't have linearizability and concurrent independent writers. PACELC made explicit: pick EC and pay in latency and single-writer topology.

notes.front: Azure Cosmos DB with multi-region writes: what conflict-resolution policies exist, and what does each imply?
notes.back:
• Last-writer-wins (LWW) (default) on _ts or a custom numeric property — simple; concurrent writes lose data silently.
  • Custom (stored procedure) — merge logic runs server-side; deterministic and bounded.
  • Manual — conflicts land in a conflicts feed for the application to resolve.
Any multi-master design is AP under partition; the policy is how you make convergence meaningful. If losing a write is unacceptable, model data so concurrent updates commute (counters, sets) or use single-region writes.

notes.front: Azure Cosmos DB replication inside a region: replica count, write commitment, and how read quorum varies.
notes.back:
Each physical partition is a replica set of 4 replicas; a write is durable once a majority (3/4) has persisted it.

Read quorum depends on consistency level: strong and bounded staleness read from a majority (or a caught-up replica via the leader's knowledge); session/eventual read from a single replica. Same R+W>N reasoning as Aurora, made dynamic per request.

notes.front: Azure Storage redundancy tiers: LRS, ZRS, GRS, RA-GRS. Which are synchronous, and what does a geo-failover cost?
notes.back:
• Locally Redundant (LRS): 3 synchronous copies, one datacenter.
  • Zone-Redundant (ZRS): 3 synchronous copies across 3 AZs — strong consistency survives an AZ loss.
  • Geo-Redundant (GRS): LRS + asynchronous copy to the paired region (RPO typically <15 min).
  • Read-Access GRS (RA-GRS): you may read the secondary — explicitly stale data.
Geo-failover (customer- or Microsoft-initiated) promotes the secondary; writes not yet replicated are lost. Sync = CP within the boundary; async = eventual across it.

notes.front: Azure Service Fabric stateful services: describe replication and the quorum loss state.
notes.back:
Each partition has a primary and N secondaries; a write is committed when a write quorum (majority) of the replica set acknowledges. Reads go to the primary → linearizable.

If fewer than a majority are up, the partition enters quorum loss: reads may continue, writes are refused until replicas return or an operator forces a (potentially lossy) recovery. A textbook CP system that refuses to guess.

notes.front: Azure Blob leases (15–60 s or infinite) are used for leader election (Dapr, Azure Functions, custom apps). What is the failure mode and the fix?
notes.back:
Same as any lease: the holder may pause (GC, VM freeze), the lease expires, another instance acquires it, and the original resumes still believing it leads.

Fix: pair the lease with a fencing mechanism — conditional writes using the blob's ETag (If-Match) or a monotonically increasing epoch stored with the lease — so a stale leader's writes are rejected rather than merely discouraged.

notes.front: Azure SQL Database failover groups: what replication mode, and what does the app need to handle?
notes.back:
Asynchronous geo-replication to a secondary region; the listener endpoint moves on failover. Because it is async, an unplanned failover can lose recent commits (RPO in seconds); a planned failover waits for sync first.

App must: use the failover-group listener (not a server name), tolerate transient connection errors with retry, and accept that read-only routing to the secondary returns slightly stale data.

notes.front: Define linearizability precisely. What scope does it apply to?
notes.back:
Every operation appears to take effect atomically at some instant between its invocation and its response, and the resulting order is consistent with real time: if op A completes before op B starts, B observes A.

Scope: a single object/register (one key, one lock). Says nothing about multi-object transactions. Equivalently: the system behaves like a single, up-to-date copy.

notes.front: Serializability vs strict serializability vs linearizability — untangle them.
notes.back:
• Serializability: multi-object transactions appear to execute in some serial order. No real-time constraint — a “serializable” system may legally serve you last week's snapshot.
  • Linearizability: single-object, real-time ordering.
  • Strict serializability = serializability + real-time order (Google Spanner's “external consistency”, via TrueTime commit-wait).
Most cloud databases that say “strongly consistent” mean linearizable per key, not strict serializable across keys.

notes.front: How does sequential consistency differ from linearizability? Give a real system that offers it.
notes.back:
Sequential: all clients see the same total order, consistent with each client's own program order — but not necessarily with real time. A client may read stale state as long as it never goes backwards.

Apache ZooKeeper: writes are linearizable (through the leader), reads are served locally by any follower → sequentially consistent; call sync() before a read to upgrade it. Kubernetes' watch cache offers the same shape.

notes.front: Define causal consistency. Why is it the strongest model achievable while remaining available under partition?
notes.back:
Writes that are causally related (one could have influenced the other — same session, or read-then-write) are observed in that order by every node; concurrent writes may be seen in different orders.

Enforcing anything stronger (e.g., a total order of concurrent writes) requires nodes on both sides of a partition to agree, which needs communication. Causal order can be tracked with vector clocks/dependency metadata locally, so it survives partitions (Bailis et al., “Highly Available Transactions”).

notes.front: List the four session guarantees and give one cloud feature that implements each.
notes.back:
• Read-your-writes — Cosmos DB session token; DynamoDB strongly consistent read after write.
  • Monotonic reads — never see older state after newer; sticky routing to one replica.
  • Monotonic writes — a client's writes apply in order; single-leader per partition.
  • Writes-follow-reads — a write depends on what you read; carry the read version (resourceVersion in Kubernetes).
Together they are “causal consistency for one client”. Cheap to provide; most user-visible anomalies come from missing them.

notes.front: Define eventual consistency rigorously. What does it not promise?
notes.back:
If no new writes occur, all replicas eventually converge to the same state.

It does not promise: when convergence happens, what any single read returns before then, that reads are monotonic, or which write wins. Convergence requires a deterministic merge rule — last-writer-wins, Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), or version vectors + application merge. Without one you have divergence, not eventual consistency.

notes.front: Last-writer-wins (LWW): why is it popular, and what are its two failure modes?
notes.back:
Popular because it is trivially convergent: keep the value with the highest timestamp.

  • Silent data loss: concurrent updates to the same key discard one entirely (two regions increment the same counter → one increment vanishes).
  • Clock dependence: a node with a fast clock “wins” the future; skew turns the newer write into the loser.
Used by DynamoDB Global Tables and Cosmos DB by default. Accept it only for keys where concurrent writes don't happen or don't matter.

notes.front: Lamport clocks vs vector clocks vs Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC): what can each detect?
notes.back:
• Lamport: a single counter; gives a total order consistent with causality (a→b ⇒ L(a)<L(b)) but cannot tell concurrency from causality.
  • Vector clocks: one counter per node; can detect that two events are concurrent (neither ≤ the other) — used by the Dynamo paper to surface conflicts instead of dropping them. Cost: O(nodes) metadata.
  • HLC: physical time + logical counter; causally consistent and close to wall-clock (CockroachDB, YugabyteDB).

notes.front: Three practical ways to get read-your-writes on top of an eventually consistent store.
notes.back:
• Route the session's reads to the leader/primary (DynamoDB strongly consistent reads; Aurora writer endpoint).
  • Carry a version/session token and require the replica to be at least that fresh (Cosmos DB session token; Kubernetes resourceVersion on list/watch).
  • Sticky routing: read from the replica you wrote to (only monotonic within that replica's lifetime).
Each shifts cost: leader load, client complexity, or lost load balancing.

notes.front: Snapshot isolation allows write skew. Give the canonical example and say what fixes it.
notes.back:
Two doctors on call; rule “at least one on call”. Both read (2 on call), both mark themselves off in concurrent transactions; neither transaction wrote what the other read, so no write-write conflict — both commit, zero on call.

Fixes: true SERIALIZABLE (PostgreSQL Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), including on Amazon RDS/Aurora PostgreSQL), or explicit locking (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) / materializing the constraint as a row.

notes.front: What does Jepsen actually test, and what is the recurring lesson from its reports?
notes.back:
It generates concurrent client histories against a real cluster while injecting faults (partitions, clock skew, process pauses), then checks the history against a model (Knossos for linearizability, Elle for transactional anomalies).

Recurring lesson: documentation claims (“strongly consistent”, “ACID”) frequently fail only under partitions or leader changes — the exact conditions consensus protocols exist for. Test under faults, or you haven't tested consistency.

notes.front: What is the CALM theorem, and how does it guide design toward coordination avoidance?
notes.back:
Consistency As Logical Monotonicity: a program has a coordination-free, eventually consistent implementation if and only if it is monotonic (outputs only grow as inputs grow — set union, append, max).

Non-monotonic operations (delete-then-check, “is this the only one?”, aggregations with negation) inherently need coordination. Design lever: reformulate as monotonic (tombstones, CRDT counters, append-only logs) and reserve consensus for the residual non-monotonic core.

notes.front: Enumerate the standard failure model hierarchy and say which one Raft/Paxos assume.
notes.back:
• Crash-stop: halts, never returns.
  • Crash-recovery: halts, returns with stable storage intact (RAM lost).
  • Omission: drops some messages (send/receive).
  • Timing: responds outside expected bounds (GC pause, slow disk).
  • Byzantine: arbitrary, including malicious.
Raft/Paxos assume crash-recovery + omission with reliable stable storage; they do not tolerate Byzantine nodes (need PBFT/3f+1) or lying disks.

notes.front: Why is “network partition” a misleadingly clean term? Describe partial and asymmetric partitions and a consensus failure they cause.
notes.back:
Real partitions are rarely a clean split. Partial: A↔B and B↔C work but A↔C doesn't. Asymmetric: A can send to B but not receive.

In Raft, a follower that can't hear the leader (but can reach others) keeps starting elections with ever-higher terms, deposing a healthy leader each time it reconnects — livelock without any node actually being down. PreVote + CheckQuorum exist for exactly this.

notes.front: Define gray failure (Huang et al.). Why do health checks miss it, and what detects it?
notes.back:
A component is degraded (partially working, slow, dropping some requests) yet passes its own health checks — differential observability: the monitor and the client see different things.

Detection must be from the client's perspective: end-to-end canaries, outlier detection/ejection in the load balancer (Envoy, Istio), request hedging, and comparing per-node error/latency against peers. AWS: “health checks are a lie unless they exercise the real path”.

notes.front: What is split brain, what two ingredients prevent it, and where does “STONITH” fit?
notes.back:
Two nodes each believe they are the sole primary and both accept writes → divergent histories.

  • Quorum: only the side with a majority may act (the minority steps down).
  • Fencing: the old primary is prevented from writing — via fencing tokens at the storage, or Shoot The Other Node In The Head (STONITH): power/network-cut the suspected node before promoting a new one.
Failover by moving a virtual IP without fencing is the classic way to get split brain.

notes.front: Why are lease-based mechanisms vulnerable to clock drift and process pauses? How does Google Spanner handle clocks differently?
notes.back:
A lease is “I'm leader until T”. If the holder's clock runs slow, or the process is paused (GC, VM live-migration, swap), local time says the lease is valid while everyone else has moved on.

Spanner's TrueTime returns an interval [earliest, latest] with GPS/atomic-clock bounded uncertainty (~ms); a transaction commit-waits until latest has passed, so timestamps are globally ordered. Uncertainty is made explicit instead of assumed away.

notes.front: A Java service holds a distributed lock, enters a 30-second stop-the-world GC, and resumes. Trace what can go wrong and what fixes it.
notes.back:
During the pause it sends no heartbeats → lock/lease expires → another instance acquires it and starts writing. The first instance wakes, has no idea time passed, and continues its critical section → two writers.

Checking “is the lock still mine?” before writing doesn't help (pause can occur between check and write). Only a fencing token validated by the resource is sound; otherwise make the operation idempotent/commutative so concurrent execution is harmless.

notes.front: What is a metastable failure? Why doesn't removing the trigger fix it?
notes.back:
A system pushed by a transient trigger (traffic spike, brief dependency slowdown) into a self-sustaining overloaded state — e.g., retries and timeouts keep effective load above capacity, or a cache flushes and every request now hits the database.

The feedback loop (retries ↑ → latency ↑ → retries ↑) sustains itself after the trigger is gone. Recovery requires actively shedding load below the sustainable level (throttle, drop retries, warm caches) — not just waiting.

notes.front: Thundering herd on cache expiry: mechanism and three mitigations.
notes.back:
A hot key expires; thousands of concurrent requests miss simultaneously and all hit the origin, which was sized for cache-hit traffic.

  • Request coalescing (singleflight): one in-flight origin fetch per key; others wait for it.
  • Probabilistic early refresh / jittered TTLs so keys don't expire in lockstep.
  • Serve-stale-while-revalidate: return the old value, refresh in background.

notes.front: Why do AWS and Azure deploy changes one Availability Zone or region at a time? Which failure class does this address?
notes.back:
Correlated failure: a bad deploy or config push is the single most common cause of large outages, and it hits every node it touches simultaneously — unlike hardware faults, which are independent.

Wave/canary deployment (AWS: one-box → one AZ → one region → waves of regions with bake time; Azure Safe Deployment Practices) converts a correlated failure into a bounded one you can roll back. Kubernetes analogue: maxUnavailable, canary via progressive delivery.

notes.front: “fsyncgate”: what did PostgreSQL discover about fsync, and what does it imply for any consensus system?
notes.back:
On Linux, if fsync fails (I/O error), the kernel may clear the dirty flag; a subsequent fsync succeeds even though the data was never written. PostgreSQL had been retrying fsync and believing the second success.

Implication: a Raft/Paxos node's “persisted to stable storage” assumption can be silently false. Correct behaviour on fsync failure is to crash (panic) and recover from a snapshot — which is what PostgreSQL and etcd now do.

notes.front: Fixed-timeout failure detectors vs the φ-accrual detector (Cassandra, Akka): what's the trade-off?
notes.back:
Any detector trades detection time against false positives; a fixed timeout picks one point on that curve for all conditions.

φ-accrual keeps a history of heartbeat intervals and outputs a continuous suspicion level (φ ≈ −log₁₀ P(heartbeat is merely late)). Callers choose their own threshold, and the detector adapts to changing network latency. Still probabilistic — no detector can be both complete and accurate in an asynchronous system.

notes.front: Two-phase commit (2PC) is blocking. Explain the failure and how Spanner-style “Paxos commit” removes it.
notes.back:
After participants vote yes (prepared) they must hold locks until the coordinator says commit/abort. If the coordinator crashes after collecting votes but before broadcasting, participants are stuck indefinitely — they can't unilaterally abort (the coordinator may have logged commit).

Fix: make the coordinator's decision itself a replicated, consensus-backed value (Spanner replicates each participant and the coordinator with Paxos; DynamoDB transactions use a durable coordinator). Blocking is replaced by “wait for the majority”.

notes.front: At-least-once vs at-most-once vs “exactly-once”: define, and state where deduplication must live.
notes.back:
• At-most-once: send once, never retry — may lose.
  • At-least-once: retry until acked — may duplicate.
  • Exactly-once processing: at-least-once delivery + idempotent or deduplicating consumer.
Dedup must live at the consumer/state owner, keyed by a client-chosen ID, with the dedup record committed atomically with the effect. Kafka transactions, SQS FIFO, EC2 client tokens all follow this shape.

notes.front: State the CAP theorem correctly (Gilbert & Lynch), and list two common misreadings.
notes.back:
In the presence of a network partition, a system cannot provide both linearizability (C) and availability (every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response) (A).

  • Misreading 1: “pick two of three” — P isn't optional; partitions happen, so the choice is only C-vs-A during one.
  • Misreading 2: C means ACID or “any consistency” — it means linearizability specifically. A system can be causally consistent and available.

notes.front: Define PACELC. Classify etcd, DynamoDB (default), Cassandra, Cosmos DB, Spanner, MongoDB.
notes.back:
If Partition: Availability vs Consistency; Else: Latency vs Consistency. Captures that strong consistency costs latency even when nothing is broken.

  • etcd / ZooKeeper / Spanner: PC/EC
  • DynamoDB default, Cassandra: PA/EL
  • Cosmos DB: configurable — strong/bounded ≈ PC/EC; session/eventual ≈ PA/EL
  • MongoDB (default write/read concern): PA/EC

notes.front: Why does strong consistency cost latency even with a perfectly healthy network? Quantify for AWS/Azure topologies.
notes.back:
A linearizable write must reach a majority before acking; a linearizable read must confirm leadership (ReadIndex) or hit the leader.

  • Cross-AZ round trip: ~1–2 ms → quorum write ≈ 2–4 ms (DynamoDB, etcd, Aurora).
  • Cross-region: 50–150 ms → Cosmos DB strong ≈ 2× RTT to the farthest region; Spanner multi-region commit tens of ms + commit-wait.
That is the “EL vs EC” axis: the price is paid on every request, not only during failures.

notes.front: Apply CAP to Kubernetes: what happens to the cluster when etcd loses quorum?
notes.back:
etcd is CP → with no majority it refuses reads (linearizable) and writes. kube-apiserver returns errors; no scheduling, scaling, rollouts, or Lease renewals.

But the data plane stays up: kubelets keep pods running, kube-proxy/CNI keep routing existing Services, DNS keeps resolving from cache. Control plane = CP; data plane = statically stable. Same layering as AWS: EC2 instances don't stop when the EC2 API does.

notes.front: Amazon Route 53 offers a 100% availability Service Level Agreement (SLA). How can that be consistent with CAP?
notes.back:
The SLA covers the data plane (answering DNS queries), which is massively replicated, anycast, and serves possibly-stale answers — an AP system. The control plane (changing records) is a separate, lower-SLA path with eventual propagation.

CAP forces C vs A only where you insist on linearizability. DNS chose A and made staleness (TTL) part of the contract.

notes.front: Harvest and yield (Fox & Brewer): a design lever CAP doesn't mention.
notes.back:
• Yield: fraction of requests answered.
  • Harvest: fraction of the data reflected in an answer.
Under partial failure you can keep yield at 100% by reducing harvest (search returns results from 9 of 10 shards, marked partial), or keep harvest and let yield drop (fail the request). Most availability engineering is choosing which to degrade per endpoint — not a binary CP/AP switch.

notes.front: Heuristic: how do you decide CP vs AP for a given piece of data?
notes.back:
Ask: “If two clients disagree about this value for a few seconds, what breaks?”

  • Nothing / self-correcting (view counts, likes, presence, caches) → AP, eventual, LWW is fine.
  • Money, uniqueness (usernames), inventory, leadership → CP per key, or restructure so the invariant is monotonic (escrow: pre-split inventory per region; CRDT counters).
Most systems are mixed: a CP core (etcd, a ledger) with AP periphery (caches, read replicas, telemetry).

notes.front: Bounded staleness is the practical middle ground. Give the staleness figure for three cloud primitives.
notes.back:
• Amazon DynamoDB eventually consistent reads: usually consistent within ~1 s.
  • Amazon Aurora read replicas: typically tens of ms behind the writer (shared storage; only cache invalidation lags).
  • Azure Cosmos DB bounded staleness: you set K versions / T seconds; Azure Storage GRS: RPO usually <15 min.
Design principle: replace “eventual” with a number and check whether the business can tolerate that number.

notes.front: Coordination is the scarce resource. Rank these by how much coordination they need: Raft write, DynamoDB eventual read, S3 PUT, CRDT counter increment, K8s pod creation.
notes.back:
• CRDT counter increment: zero — local op, merges later.
  • DynamoDB eventual read: none beyond routing to a replica.
  • S3 PUT: strongly consistent index update — coordinated metadata write, but per-key.
  • Raft write (etcd put): majority round trip + fsync.
  • K8s pod creation: Raft write plus a chain of controllers (scheduler, kubelet) each doing further CAS writes — many sequential consensus rounds.
Latency and availability ceilings follow this ranking almost exactly.
